19. Cubicle (q): the painting (here in the reproduction of the diSUC by G. Mariani executed in 1890) belongs to the group of representations of the myth of Daedalus and Icarus that dwell on the moment of the tragic flight; it is indeed the oldest of the replicas deriving from a Roman original, reworked in the last decades of the first century BC from a pre-existing Hellenistic tradition. The presence of some details that are not functional to the narrative (such as the statue of Poseidon, the fisherman on the shore) or that will not return in other replicas (the view of Knossos) proves that the Rione has referred to a previous model. In the painting in question we find a typical representation of the early III style with small characters, among which one of the Aktai is of classicist reference, which reproduces the type of Polyhymnia, immersed in the landscape that almost becomes dominant with the islands in the distance, the rocky coast in the foreground and the tree. Even Helios on the quadriga, from which the bright mortal rays radiate, has no particular prominence; rather appears to be the protagonist (as in the replicas of Group I, cf. Blanckenhagen), Daedalus with a long robe (inspired by Hellenistic depictions of Victory, the model of winged figure par excellence) which contributes to giving composure to his quiet flight, contrasting with the precipitous fall of Icarus. Dependent on the notoriety in Pompeii of Ovid's poetry (Ars Am., 2, 85; id., Met., 8, 126 ff.) is the predilection for depictions in painting of this mythical episode, in which the drama is heightened by the fact that one of the protagonists is unaware that the tragedy has already taken place.

21. Cubicle (q), painting of wall E in a drawing by G. Mariani. In a mountainous landscape, three hunters with skewers and dogs approach a simulacrum of Artemis-Isis, erected in a grove, near a betilo surmounted by a radiated crown. One of them, in which Hippolytus was recognized, offers a crown to the statue of the goddess; a little further back is another female statue (Aphrodite, to whom the young man refuses homage) standing near another betilo surmounted by an element that is not clearly distinguishable (a cyst?); on the right there is a large tripod, a reference to Apollo, placed on a round base. In the background, between cliffs and bushes, another betilo, while halfway up the composition a deer jumps that seems to come out of a cave. Although the landscape element is decidedly predominant and can make the painting interpreted as a simple sacred landscape, the decorative program of the cubicle made explicit in the comparison of the two pairs of paintings (Daedalus and Icarus / Marsyas, Hippolytus / Heracles and the Hesperides), leans towards the mythological subject, of which this is the only representation known so far, rather than for a generic landscape representation.

22. Cubicle (q): the painting (now in the National Museum of Naples, inv. 120626) with a representation of the myth of Marsyas (also in this case it is the only replica that has come down to us), is an example of continuous narration to be read, on the left from top to bottom and on the right from bottom to top, in which the progress of events does not correspond to an exacerbation of dramatic tension,  although the motionless figures in the background, almost immersed in the landscape, do not bode well. Athena, seated by a pond, helmeted and with her shield next to her, plays the double flute while a nymph, half-emerging from the water, holds a mirror in front of her and a figure with a cornucopia sits on the shore. Marsyas, covered only with the cloak hanging behind his shoulders and with the pedum, watches the scene from above; he then moves away from the shore after picking up the instrument thrown by the goddess and then, playing it, approaches, almost running, a group of not very distinct figures, among which a seated woman stands out, dressed in a long yellow chiton (Apollo and the Muses?). Also in this painting, the landscape setting is an integral part of the scene: from the rocks among which Marsyas wanders, to the column adorned with bandages near the lake, to the plain in which the Silenus runs, to the walled buildings in the background, next to the Muses. As in the painting with the flight of Daedalus and Icarus, Gegenstiick on the N wall, the tragic conclusion of the story is not represented, but there are all the premises for the divinity to punish those who have acted arrogantly towards him.

23. Cubicle (q), wall O with the door and the circular splayed window, which takes light from the peristyle (t). Few traces remain of the decoration with a black plinth and a red middle area, in which was the painting with Heracles and the Hesperides.

24. Cubicle (q): the drawing by G. Discanno, together with another by G. Mariani are the only reproductions of the painting now completely lost, of which, already in 1928, only "a few evanescent traces of color" remained (Elia Rend.Linc. 1928, p. 176). In a mountainous and wooded landscape, the three Hesperides tame the serpent Ladon, who wraps himself around an altar, to allow Heracles to pluck the three apples. The hero is naked, with the lion on his arm, the bow and quiver on the left and the club in the right. Although the model to which this and the other known replica of the same subject refer (from House I 7,7) is unique, in the present painting it seems that the effort has not yet been accomplished: although it is difficult to determine whether or not he has the apples in his hand, it seems that he holds the club and does not keep it abandoned. Here, above all, the landscape setting is extensive, absent in the other painting: we find, in addition to the large tree, functional to the narrative, rocks, bushes, trees and branches, a column surmounted by an urn and a cubic construction that acts as a backdrop behind the figure of Heracles. Coupled with the opposite painting with Hippolytus, an example of modesty, in the context of the decorative program of the small cubicle, this one with Heracles and the Hesperides is a demonstrative subject of the happy outcome of actions guided by prudence and an attitude respectful of the divine will.

1. Atrium (A), wall N. In the photograph, taken by the American archaeologist Esther B. Van Deman a few years after the excavation, in 1914, the excellent state of preservation of the plaster allows us to fully appreciate the liveliness and immediacy of this kind of paintings, always the same and yet always different in the variety of combinations of the elements they recur. The lararium is painted on a white background and depicts, among quickly painted bushes, an agathodaìmon serpent approaching the altar of the sacrifice on which the offerings are placed, painted as usual in imitation of marble. On bases, also imitating marble, are represented the statues of the Lares, which as usual are arranged symmetrically, holding in their hands atera and rhytòn and framing a niche intended for their worship, bordered by a frame painted with palmettes. Inside the niche you can see the small marble altar, devoid of decoration, found in it. The building events mentioned in the Introduction to this house suggest the dating of this painting to the last years of Pompeii's life. FU 10707F

1. Peristyle (n), S portico in front of (m), with the corner column S-E incorporated into the W wall of (m), testifying to the construction renovations that have mainly affected this part of the house. A lararium is painted in the niche: between the plants of the hoof an agathodaimon snake wraps its coils; the rituals of sacrifice are alluded to by the double flute player next to the sacrificing genius with cornucopia, depicted within the niche, while the honored deities are represented by the Lares painted on the sides of the niche (the one on the left is painted on the walled column of the peristyle, the one on the right is illegible). On the left is also depicted the victim pushing the pig to be sacrificed. On the lower part of the column is depicted Mercury, with bag, caduceus and petasus. The figures are painted according to the typical modules of 'plebeian' art, which are often adopted in paintings of religious subjects.  The lararium was intended to be repainted: in fact, a slight rinsing had been applied to it, evidence that this kind of painting was frequently redone in ancient times with the simple superimposition of a coat of lime, without the more complex expedients that were normally adopted to facilitate the adhesion of the new plaster on the layer of paint that was intended to be abolished. The decoration, which has almost completely lost the last layer of color, consisted of a black plinth, above which was a middle area with a yellow central panel and red side panels, separated by narrow compartments with a black background. In the center of the panels were painted vignettes, like the one in the previous figure, which was on the stretch of wall on the left in the photo. In the decorative program of the atrium it was evidently intended to honor all the deities: on the S wall, in fact, at the time of the excavation, a vignette with a panther, an animal sacred to Bacchus, was seen in the center, while in the side panels there were avoni, sacred to Juno. IV stie. The upper area is rough. On the right, the plaster follows the course of the staircase that led to the rooms on the upper floor. 79 N49130

caption_en: 3. Atrium (B). This marble statue of a panther (an animal sacred to Dionysus) crouched down, with eyes inserted in glass paste, served as a support for the table; The terracotta cistern mouth, with caryatids between two ovule cornices in the upper part, dates back to the Republican age. These typical atrium furnishings have since been removed from the house for safety reasons.

The plinth is red, without any other decoration (Sogliano NS 1905, p. 134); in the middle area there are two black panels, on the sides of the narrow and high central aedicule with a red background, supported by slender columns, which suggests a dating to the third style. In the fields of the middle zone there was no decoration.

caption_en: 15. Cubicle (H), wall N. At the front of the room is a panel with a white background bordered by red-line carpet edges. A red band, which seems to recall the columns or pilasters painted in this same spot in the cubicles of the late Republican age, marks the passage to the innermost space, reserved for the bed, of which the recess is visible. In the alcove, the middle area, also white, is divided into two parts by a central compartment with a candelabra, on the sides of which are two panels with vignettes. Also different between the two parts of the room was the roof, which was lower in the alcove. The decoration is repeated identically on the wall in front of S. IV style.

caption_en: 18. Cubicle (I), floor. The cocciopesto carpet departs from the compositional sobriety of the Republican specimens to accommodate a dense ornamentation of white tesserae, arranged according to a motif typical of the contemporary mosaic repertoire, the network of diamonds and squares. A row of white tesserae delimits the carpet, bordered by a low band of scattered white tesserae.

19. Cubicle (I), wall N. The wall, corresponding to the antechamber with a flat ceiling of the room, has a yellow plinth and a white middle area, with panels bordered by carpet edges. In the center of the wall was depicted a griffin in flight, now disappeared. IV style.

20. Cubicle (I), S. wall The space of the alcove, enclosed by a low decorative vault bordered at the bottom by a molded frame, is painted with a yellow plinth and a middle area with white panels bordered by carpet edges, which contained a vignette with a griffin in the center, vignettes with swans on the sides. In the vault (Sogliano NS 1905, p. 134) there was instead a rural scene with grazing pigs. IV style.

21. Cubicle (I), W wall with rectangular splayed window overlooking the alley. Remains of the IV style decoration on a white background. Above the cubicle, the front of the house housed a second floor, accessible from the staircase mentioned in fig. 3, of which the holes left by the beams of the floor can be seen, below which are also visible, in the plaster preparation layer, large fragments of shards, inserted to quickly equalize the preparation layer itself.
22. Viridarium (K), E face, section N. In the niche, as in the whole viridarium, plants were painted that illusionistically dilated the very small space of the garden. 79 N49129

The decoration was repeated the same on the other walls. IV style.

caption_en: 1. Atrium (b), wall O, on which was a richly decorated lararium. Above the plinth and a paneled plinth with plants and birds, separated by narrow compartments with stylized candelabra, is a frieze with a procession of deities: on the left Mercury with petasus and caduceus, at whose feet are the rooster and the omphalòs, around which a snake wraps itself; followed by a winged Victory who is preparing to crown Hercules who, in addition to the club and the lion's skin, also carries the bow in his left; at his feet is the little pig to be sacrificed; at the right end is Minerva libante, with helmet, shield and spear, near which, on a small pillar, is the owl sacred to her. In the upper register, within a small aedicule whose tympanum is adorned with a laurel wreath in stucco relief, there is the niche, flanked by the figure of Pompeian Venus (on the left, collapsed), and by Fortune with cornucopia. Outside the aedicule, on the left, remains of the figure of Bacchus giving drink to the panther crouching at his feet, on the right Jupiter enthroned. In the upper area, on a white background, aiati of the stucco patera symbolizing sacrifice, are painted two eagles in flight with a palm branch, the bird sacred to Jupiter, framed in turn by Juno's peacock (preserved only on the right), perched on a garland. The scheme within which the decoration is inserted is that of the walls of the IV style.
2. Atrium (b), O wall. Detail of the plinth and frieze with procession of deities. AFS C1853
3. Atrium (b), wall O: current state of conservation of the lararium illustrated in the previous figures.
4. Tablinum (b'), wall N. Remains of the IV style painting, with red plinth, middle area and upper yellow area. IV style.  79 N49077

8. Triclinium (d), N wall: detail of the architectural foreshortening with a white background, closed by a high pluteus with block masonry, which separates the central panel of the middle area from the left one. IV style.
9. 'Triclinium (d), N wall, section O: remains of a Gorgon mask hanging above the foreshortening reproduced in the previous figure.

11. Triclinium (d), wall E, section N. Of the medallions with cupids which, according to the excavation report, were found in the side panels of the middle area, only the trace engraved with the compass remains, while the figuration has completely disappeared.

10. Triclinium (d), wall E. Yellow plinth, white middle area, which bore in the center a painting, completely vanished, with the figure of Narcissus, and in the side panels medallions with cupids; white upper area. IV style.
12. Triclinium (d), S wall: yellow base; White middle area: central panel with painting and side panel with medallion, separated by an architectural foreshortening. IV style. 79 N49042
14. Triclinium (d), $S wall, section E. Remains of the architectural foreshortening that divides the central panel and the side panel of the middle area.

13. Triclinium (d), S wall, section E. White middle area: remains of the medallion with griffin in flight that adorned the white side panel. The frame of the medallion is between two circles, engraved with a compass. IV style.

16. Triclinium (d), S wall, central section: detail of the head of Dionysus with a crown of vine on his head, painted with broad brushstrokes and impressionistic touches of white, not without effect. IV style. 79 N49039

15. Triclinium (d), S wall, central section. The theme depicted in this painting (the epiphany of Dionysus, god of wine, who finds Ariadne asleep: Dionysus and, at the bottom, Ariadne's head remain partially visible) is particularly suitable for the decoration of a triclinium room. Above the painting there is a palmette in the center and, on the sides, shoots with volutes. IV style.

17. Triclinium (f), N-W angle. Of the decoration of this room, open to the garden (m), only this fragment of the middle area is preserved, which was adorned with a yellow panel arranged in such a way as to simulate the effect of a carpet stretched at the corners, bordered by a garland and framed by carpet edges. According to the excavation report, it also painted medallions with cupids with gladiatorial weapons, of which there is no longer any trace. IV style.

18. Kitchen (n), wall E. Of the second lararium existing in this house, reproduced in NS 1901, p. 258, fig. 2, which arranged food and kitchen utensils in three registers (from bottom to top); a large serpent; remains
1. View of the workshop accessible from entrance no. 7, with a jamb of limestone blocks. The façade was protected by a canopy, which also covered the adjacent entrance, no. 6.
2. On the N of the shop at no. 7, outside the room (c), evidently intended for patrons (see fig. 3), the God of wine was depicted, under a vine pergola, leaning on a Satyr playing the zither.

3. Room (c), wall N. The simple decoration of the room is a two-part scheme with a white background: the plinth is bordered by purple bands; in the center of the middle area is a candelabra, the side panels are bordered by simple carpet borders; the upper area was also white. The decoration was repeated identically on the other walls. IV style.

4. Jamb N between rooms (d) and (e): the figure of Venus Pompeiana accompanied by a cupid, here painted on a red background, was entrusted with the protection of the wine that aged in the dolii buried in the wine cellar behind (f), visible in the background.

5. Jab S between rooms (d) and (e): the figure of Venus painted on the jamb in front is supported by the figure of Mercury who, holding his bag in his right hand, was to encourage the earnings that the inhabitants of this house obtained from the sale of wine in shop no. 7.

1-2. Atrium (c), N wall, W section. In the N-W corner of the room, within a rectangular panel of cocciopesto, this small niche for the cult of the Lares has been inserted, covered by a triangular tympanum and outlined by polychrome stucco frames (white, red and green) with ornamentation of lotuses and trefoils. In the photo you can see the eight-pointed stars, red and green, which adorn the 'sky' of the niche. Inside the niche were found a bronze bust of Minerva, an alabaster Venus and an ivory male figure.

1-2. Atrium (c), N wall, W section. In the N-W corner of the room, within a rectangular panel of cocciopesto, this small niche for the cult of the Lares has been inserted, covered by a triangular tympanum and outlined by polychrome stucco frames (white, red and green) with ornamentation of lotuses and trefoils. In the photo you can see the eight-pointed stars, red and green, which adorn the 'sky' of the niche. Inside the niche were found a bronze bust of Minerva, an alabaster Venus and an ivory male figure.
3. Cubicle (h), S. Wall Remains of wall decoration of the first style, in stucco relief, datable to the Republican age.

2. Façade, section N, to the right of the door. On the jamb in front of it, on the other hand, the stormy sea was depicted, populated by dolphins, on which the crew of a small boat risked their lives. Combined with the representation of Mercury, the latter figuration seems to allude to the danger of "maritime trade", in which the owner of the house must have been involved, who has been identified, on the basis of the seal found in this house, with M. Fabius Secundus, a character who appears, both as buyer and as witness, in the wax tablets of the archive of L. Caecilius Giocondo V 1,  26. from T. Warsher, Pompeji, Berlin-Leipzig 1925, fig. 29

1. Façade, section S, to the left of the door: on the high plinth of cocciopesto is painted, as an auspicious sign outside the house, the figure of Mercury, with a bag and caduceus in his hands; at his feet is the omphalòs, around which a snake is wrapped. The sign can be read more clearly in a drawing preserved at the Swedish Institute in Rome.

3. 'Triclinium (R), N. wall, the painting reproduced in the following figures has been detached from the wall for its iconographic interest, while the rest of the decoration, already in poor condition at the time of the excavation, has been abandoned to progressive deterioration. The painting, datable to the last phase of the III style, has a symmetrical scheme: above the black plinth in the center is an aedicule, flanked by red side panels, above which was a yellow frieze; the upper area is also red.
4. 'Triclinio (R), N wall, central section: the aedicule with the painting depicting the origins of Rome, in situ before the detachment. III style, phase II B. AFSN B3257
5. Painting depicting the origins of Rome (Museo Naz. Naples, without inv. number). The painting depicts Mars in arms who descends to meet Rhea Silvia, asleep and therefore blameless

6. Painting with the origins of Rome: detail of the upper section, with Mars armed. The chariot on the left alludes to the moment in which the action takes place, but according to the various commentators it is not possible to determine whether it is the chariot of the Sun or the Moon.
7. Painting with the origins of Rome: detail of the lower area, in which Mercury points to a female figure (Rhea Silvia or Venus), the she-wolf and the twins.
8. Triclinium (R), N wall, central section: in the upper red area, above the aedicule, there is a small picture with masks, completely vanished, next to which a slight aedicule can be recognized.

9. Triclinium (R), wall E, section N: between the red panels of the middle area there is a white compartment containing a vegetable candelabrum: in the upper red area there are light architectures represented in perspective, typical of the final phase of the III style (see for example vol. I, p. 937, fig. 30, House 19, 1).

10. Triclinium (R), W wall, S section. The decoration is mirrored to that of the previous figure; in the center, remains of the aedicule, of which the coffered ceiling can still be glimpsed. III style, phase II B.

11. Triclinium (R), W wall, section N. The function of the room is ensured by the recessed for the existing bed. Through the large hole filled by the restoration, ancient prospectors have penetrated the house.

12. Triclinium (R), fragment of plaster, most likely collapsed from the upper area, with a red background. The color has completely fallen, allowing the vertical guide lines to emerge that indicate the trace of the columns of an annular portico, in which, as in House I 9, 1 (cf. vol. I, p. 930, fig. 18), imagines clipeatae, of which only a very thin trace can be glimpsed, were fixed to horizontal beams; the subject of the central picture is no longer identifiable.

1. Peristyle (d), overall view from S-W: the columns, six on the short sides and eight on the long sides, are covered in white stucco and joined by an open parapet at the entrance (b) and the access to the triclinium (s). At his feet runs a red hoof; It remains difficult to establish whether the original decoration of the parapet was entirely in red plaster to connect with the red stucco decoration of the columns. Mau supposed a simultaneous renovation of the columns which were covered in white stucco and of the parapet which was adorned with paintings of the fourth style.

2. Peristyle (d), portico E, first internal pluteus from N: largely damaged already at the time of the excavation, the panel shows a building on a platform with a balustrade within a seabed where, scarcely visible, there are three small boats. IV style.

3. Peristyle (d), portico E, second internal pluteus from N: on the right Europa, with a cloak covering her shoulders and legs, on the bull; in tow are two Nereids, one seated on a sea horse, the other on a dolphin. In the background rocks and sea. A plant motif decoration behind a gate is present on the columns. IV style.  79 N49021

4. Peristyle (d), portico E, third internal pluteus from N with cistern mouth; two other cisterns, with puteals covered with red plaster, were located on the W side of the garden. The panel shows a seabed with fish. IV style.
5. Peristyle (d), portico E, fourth internal pluteus from N; frame with a red background with plant motifs; in the center of the panel a panther chased by two greyhounds. IV style.

6. Peristyle (d), portico W, first internal pluteus from N: in the panel, lower left, on the shore, it is a fisherman; above high cliffs there is a small colonnaded building and a sacellum, in the center you can see Icarus and on the left Daedalus, at the top Helios with the chariot. IV style.
7. Peristyle (d), W portico, second internal pluteus from N; in the panel, at the bottom, a wild boar attacked by a dog and confronted by another; above, a deer and a dog facing each other. IV style.

8. Peristyle (d), West portico, third internal pluteus from N; the panel, very ruined, shows on the left a deer chased by a dog and on the right a bear in the act of getting up to pick fruit from a tree; in the background there are traces of a sacred landscape. IV style.

9. Peristyle (d), West portico, fourth internal pluteus from N; in the panel a large figure of a wild boar hunted by dogs; on the right, an attempt has been made to render the animal figures in perspective. IV style.

10. Peristyle (d), West portico, fifth internal pluteus from N; in the center of the panel a lion facing left, faced by a dog, while another bites it from behind; in the background a deer chased by a dog. IV style.

11. Peristyle (d), W portico, sixth internal pluteus from N with cistern mouth; in the panel, almost completely vanished, there was a scene of deer and bear hunting; currently only a dog on the right is recognizable. IV style.

12. Room (h), wall E; The low plinth and the middle area of the decoration are recognizable, consisting of red panels with two-line carpet edges, separated by a compartment with a black background. IV style.
13. Room (i), wall N: plinth scarcely legible with squares; the middle area is almost completely vanished (the tripartition lines can be distinguished). III style.
14. Room (i), wall E: red plinth; black middle area with panels separated by white bands; in the center cartoons, now illegible. III style.
15. Room (i), wall S: the decorative syntax is repeated in the same way as that of wall N, for which cf. fig. 13. ITI style.
16. Room (i), wall W, section N with door facing the peristyle (d): plaster minimally preserved; Distinguishable part of the red hoof, green band and black middle area. III style.
17. Room (1), N wall, section W: red plinth scarcely legible.
18. Room (1), wall E, fresco almost completely vanished; red hoof; tripartite black (?) middle area.
19. Room (l), wall O, section S with access door to the peristyle (d): red plinth, green band; black middle area. Mau attributed the decorations, then legible, to the III style of candelabra.

20. Esedra (m), wall E, section N, middle area: yellow orthostats with parallel lines identifying the panels, hanging pine garland in the centre; upper area: row of faux marble ashlars, gurate corbels (Centaurs, Satyrs and Maenads) supporting the white frame of the coffered ceiling, row of purple ashlars placed at the head; on the right side a white column in front of the decoration. II style, phase II A. 78 N47261
21. Exedra (m), wall E, section N: detail of fig. previous.

22. Triclinium (n): overall view of the floor of the antechamber and room in black and white mosaic with polychrome tiles; in the foreground the carpet of the antechamber, poorly preserved, with a band of leaves and berries; the threshold has a laced circle pattern; the floor of the room shows a large carpet with corner palmettes from which shoots branch off within circled edges divided into segments, broken by horizontal lines, alternating with opposing semicircles and crossed by lanceolate leaves; the central emblem, very ruined, has a Hellenistic rosette with a two-strand braid border between black and white bands. The floor decoration seems to be coeval with the wall decoration.

23. Triclinium (n), floor of the antechamber: the flounce with a motif of leaves and berries, tied at the corners by a ribbon, within black and white bands, recalls a similar motif in the cubicle (z) of the House of the Silver Wedding (V 2, i); The carpet, very poorly preserved, has orange globular elements on a pedestal (vases?) and shoots. III style, phase I A.
24. Triclinium (n), floor, detail of the threshold between the antechamber and the hall; Black and white mosaic with laced circles pattern. III style, phase I A.

25. Triclinium (n), floor of the hall, corner N-W; detail of the black and white mosaic border with the use of polychrome tiles: circles divided into segments broken by horizontal lines, alternating with opposing semicircles, crossed by six lanceolate leaves.

26. 'Triclinium (n), floor of the room, black and white mosaic with the use of polychrome tiles; Carpet: central emblem with Hellenistic rosette (with palmettes and pelte inscribed) within a two-stranded braid border between black and white bands. III style, phase I A.

27. Triclinium (n), floor of the hall, corner N-W; black and white mosaic with the use of polychrome tiles: border in circles divided into segments broken by horizontal lines, alternating with opposing semicircles, crossed by six lanceolate leaves: in the carpet angular palmetto from which shoots branch off.
28. Triclinium (n), overall view of the antechamber, walls E and S, the latter with plaster almost completely vanished; to the O access to the peristyle (d).  78 N47269

29. Triclinium (n), wall E: the fluted stucco pilaster serves as a dividing element between the antechamber and the hall, where, in the white middle area, the S side panel shows a Maenad with thyrsus and tambourine. III style, phase I A.  AFSC 1676

31. Triclinium (n), wall E, antechamber: poorly preserved black plinth; black middle area, between white bands, in the center of which a female herm supports a garland; upper black area: two female heads ending in scrolls.
30. Triclinium (n), wall E: fluted stucco pilaster, with traces of a Corinthian capital, which serves as a dividing element between the antechamber and the hall.
32. Triclinium (n), wall E, antechamber: detail of the previous figure.
33. Triclinium (n), wall E, section S, antechamber: detail of the upper black area: female head ending in shoots. III style, phase IA.
34. Triclinium (n), S wall, section E, antechamber, upper black area: female head ending in shoots within a frame. III style, phase IA.
35. Triclinium (n), S wall, section O, antechamber: upper black area: female head with wings placed within a frame. III style, phase I A.

36. Triclinium (n), wall N, section O, upper area, room: above a dividing band that separates the middle area from the upper white area, runs along the entire room, a small metal copper gate near which is a Silenus carrying a cup in his right hand and a branch ending in a star motif in his left raised:  above the red band. III style, phase IA.
37. Triclinium (n), N wall, section O, room: detail of the upper white area with the figure of Silenus at the gate. III style, phase I A.

38. Triclinium (n), wall E, central section: the white middle area is divided into three parts by green candelabra that continue into the upper area; in the center is a garland with a hanging ribbon; in the S side panel there is a Maenad with thyrsus and tambourine; the upper area is characterized by a molded frame on which rests a branched gate, in the fields stand female figures wrapped in large cloaks, the central one seated on a base ending in volutes, the side S holds a zither in her hands; on the capitals of the candelabra are winged female figures; a fluted pilaster divides the decoration of the room from that of the antechamber for which cf. figs. 29-31.

39. Triclinium (n), wall E, room: plinth with orthostats arranged at the head and cut, red moulded band; middle area with a white background tripartite by thread-like green candelabra that continue in the upper area; in the center hangs a garland wrapped in a ribbon, in the side panels female figures; yellow moulded frame, frieze with flowers, small gate; white upper area: winged female figures stand on the capitals of the candelabra, in the central field there is a seated female figure, on the sides female figures, on bases, holding stringed instruments in their hands.
40. Triclinium (n), wall E, section N, room; detail of the white middle area: draped female figure with plate in her left hand and branch in the right.
41. Triclinium (n), wall E, section S, room; detail of the white middle area: Maenad waving a tambourine with his left hand and raising a thyrsus with his right. III style, phase IA. 78 N47270
